question: Lambda Architecture is defined by which core structural idea?
options: Parallel batch and speed (streaming) layers whose outputs are merged in a serving layer
A single streaming layer that handles all processing
A purely batch system with no real-time component
Serverless functions triggered per event only
explanation: Lambda runs a batch layer (accurate, reprocessable views over all data) alongside a speed layer (low-latency views over recent data). A serving layer merges them so queries get both completeness and freshness.

question: What is the primary purpose of the batch layer in Lambda Architecture?
options: To provide sub-second latency for the newest events
To recompute comprehensive, authoritative views from the full immutable master dataset, correcting any speed-layer approximations
To store only the most recent hour of data
To replace the serving layer entirely
explanation: The batch layer periodically recomputes accurate views over the complete historical master dataset. Because it reprocesses everything, it is fault-tolerant and self-correcting; the speed layer only covers the gap until the next batch run.

question: The most commonly cited drawback of Lambda Architecture is:
options: It cannot handle high data volumes
It has no way to serve real-time results
The need to implement and maintain the same business logic twice, in both the batch and speed codebases
It requires strong consistency across all replicas
explanation: Because batch and speed layers use different frameworks yet must produce equivalent results, teams often duplicate logic and struggle to keep the two implementations in sync, a key motivation for Kappa Architecture.

question: In Lambda Architecture, the master dataset feeding the batch layer is ideally:
options: Mutable and frequently updated in place
Discarded after each batch run to save space
Stored only in the speed layer's in-memory cache
An immutable, append-only record of raw events
explanation: An immutable, append-only master dataset means the batch layer can always recompute correct views by reprocessing from raw data, and errors are fixed by replaying rather than mutating stored records.

question: How does the serving layer typically reconcile results from the batch and speed layers for a query?
options: It merges the accurate batch view with the incremental speed view covering the period the batch has not yet processed
It returns whichever layer responds first and ignores the other
It always ignores the speed layer for correctness
It recomputes everything from raw events on each query
explanation: The serving layer combines the authoritative batch view (all data up to the last batch run) with the speed layer's real-time increment for events since that run, giving both accuracy and low latency.
